mn115:2.1: _Paṇḍita_ is normally used for a learned scholar, rather than a contemplative “sage”. Pali has many more terms for “a wise person” than does English, and it is not easy to distinguish the senses. “Astute” is meant to convey the sense of one who is observant and of sound judgment.
mn115:3.2: Notice the different approaches used by Ānanda and Sāriputta in the previous discourse. Sāriputta took up the Buddha’s teaching and elaborated it, whereas Ānanda uses inquiry to prompt the Buddha himself to speak further.
mn115:4.1: As emphasized in this sutta, the notion of an “element” (_dhātu_) is a flexible one, including a range of different properties, qualities, or aspects of existence.
mn115:4.2: These eighteen elements are mentioned only twice elsewhere in the Suttas ([sn14.1:2.2](), [sn41.2:3.10]()), and hundreds of times in the Abhidhamma, where they are classified specifically as an Abhidhamma teaching ([vb3:32.1]()).
mn115:4.8: The “mind element” (_manodhātu_) is not defined in the Suttas. See [mn28:37.1]() and note there. The Abhidhamma Vibhaṅga says that the mind element arises immediately after a sense impression or engagement with mental phenomena or “ideas” ([vb3:48.2]()), and the mind consciousness element arises immediately after the corresponding mind element ([vb3:55.2]()).
mn115:5.1: The method of building a lengthy discourse by asking for “another way” of exposition is also used at [mn9](), [sn44.6](), [an5.106](), and [snp3.12]().
mn115:10.1: Ānanda moves on to the next topic, the six senses. Perhaps this move was prompted by the mention of the “unconditioned element” of Nibbāna, signifying that that method of analysis had reached its culmination.
mn115:12.1: Said to be one of the ten powers of a Realized One ([mn12:10.1](), [an10.22:3.3]()), and to be restricted to those with meditative immersion (_samādhi_, [an6.64:13.1]()). Each item here, split into separate suttas, is found at [an1.168]()–295. Briefer examples of this trope are found at [mn122:3.2](), [sn12.30](), [an6.70](), and [an6.93](). These all focus on cause and effect as it pertains to development of the path.
mn115:12.2: A stream-enterer (or above) might unthinkingly act as if something were permanent (etc.), but on reflection they would know right away that this is not the case. | This passage largely mirrors [an1.268]()-295.
mn115:13.1: Murder of mother, father, or an arahant, injuring a Buddha, and causing schism are said to be specially heinous deeds that result in rebirth in hell ([an5.129]()).
mn115:13.9: This does not mean that they cannot learn from another teacher; rather, they know that the Buddha’s path leads to liberation because they have realized it for themselves.
mn115:14.1: A _lokadhātu_ is a single system with an earth, a sun and moon, planets, and a set of heavenly realms. Thus with due allowance for the different context, it is similar to a “solar system”. While many Buddhas may arise in the same solar system, they may not arise in the same region at the same time. There may, however, be many Buddhas simultaneously throughout the galaxy, an idea developed in later texts (eg. Mahāvastu 1.122).
mn115:14.3: A wheel-turning monarch was conceived as establishing dominion over the entire land from ocean to ocean, which apparently was believed to be the civilized world at the time the myth was created.
mn115:15.1: This section asserts that a women cannot fulfill the roles of foremost leadership, whether spiritual (Buddha), earthly (wheel-turning monarch), or heavenly (Sakka, Māra, and Brahmā). The Buddha lived in a patriarchal society where female leadership at this level was unknown, and it is perhaps assumed that people would not follow a woman in that role; a similar argument is made today for why a woman should not be chosen as Presidential candidate. Similar reasoning may be behind the idea that a Buddha is born either an aristocrat or a brahmin, whichever is the leading class of the time ([dn14:1.5.1]()). Still, this does not explain why such a statement would be made. It is of no spiritual relevance, since a woman may realize full liberation as an arahant in this very life. It cannot be about a woman making a vow to be a Buddha in the future, as no such vow is found anywhere in early Buddhism. It is also hard to understand how this knowledge can be a form of insight, since it depends on social structures and customary beliefs that arose in particular historical conditions. The Chinese parallel of the Bahudhātukasutta at MA 181 lacks this passage entirely, while other parallels exhibit inconsistencies and a tendency to growth over time (Anālayo, “The Bahudhātuka-sutta and its Parallels”, Journal of Buddhist Ethics, vol 16, 2009). Most likely these passages were added at a time when female leadership in the Saṅgha was contested, for which see [an8.51]() and notes.
mn115:15.5: While we encounter these divinities as individuals, they are understood as being stations or offices in the leading role of their particular realms. Thus, for example, Moggallāna said that he used to be Māra in a past life ([mn50:8.1]()).
mn115:18.1: The qualification “for that reason” (_taṁnidānā tappaccayā_) is essential, as it is quite possible for someone to engage in bad conduct and later take a good rebirth due to other deeds. This case is discussed in [mn136:18.1]().
mn115:20.4: The “four rounds” are the four main topics (elements, sense fields, dependent origination, the possible and the impossible); elsewhere it is said to be the four noble truths ([sn22.56:2.1]()). | The “mirror of the teaching” is the ability of a noble one to see the truth of the Dhamma in themselves ([sn55.8:5.1](), [dn16:2.8.3]()). | The “drum of freedom from death” was sounded by the Buddha after his awakening ([mn26:25.21]()). | The “supreme victory in battle” was also suggested as a title for the Brahmajālasutta ([dn1:3.74.3]()), while elsewhere it is said to be a name for the noble eightfold path ([sn45.4:4.3]()).
